terms.grammar: ablative of the way, with a verb of going: the hill that faces the walker
evidence: Caes. BG 2.19: eādem autem celeritāte adversō colle ad nostra castra … contendērunt
Sall. Jug. 52: adversō colle, sīcutī praeceptum fuerat, ēvādunt
terms.comment: How Caesar and Sallust send men up a hill. With a verb of climbing the hill can be the object instead: collem ascendere, clīvum superāre.

evidence: Sen. Ep. 40.7: quemadmodum per prōclīve currentium nōn ubi vīsum est gradus sistitur
terms.comment: Of the slope itself Terence’s Syrus says clīvos deorsum vorsum est, “the slope runs downhill” (Ad. 574–575).

phrases.latin: Adversō colle lentē ascendimus; dā mihi manum.
phrases.english: We’re going slowly up the hill; give me your hand.

phrases.latin: Nōlī per prōclīve currere, nē cadās.
phrases.english: Don’t run down the hill, or you’ll fall.

phrases.latin: mīlia tum prānsī tria rēpimus atque subīmus inpositum saxīs lātē candentibus Anxur
phrases.english: then, after lunch, we crawled three miles and climbed up to Anxur, perched on its far-gleaming rocks

phrases.latin: ita leviter et sēnsim clīvō fallente cōnsurgit, ut cum ascendere tē nōn putēs, sentiās ascendisse
phrases.english: the slope rises so gently and gradually, without your noticing, that when you don’t think you are climbing, you find you have climbed

sources: Lewis & Short: adversus · Lewis & Short: proclivis · Lewis & Short: declivis
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 306, 400.
